story.title: A neighbourhood bar with a trattoria kitchen
body: Bar Capri sits in the Esquilino district, on Via Principe Amedeo, where Romans walk to work every morning and travellers arrive straight off the train. We serve both the same way: good ingredients, honest portions, clear prices.

In the kitchen we stay with Roman tradition: crisp guanciale, pecorino grated to order, artichokes in season. At the oven we work a dough that matures for twenty-four hours, because a pizza should be easy to digest.
Guests with particular needs will find gluten-free bread, pasta, pizza and dessert, and a vegan and vegetarian list that is a real choice, not an afterthought.

story.title: Simple, done well, every day
body: We opened on Via Principe Amedeo because it is a street that never sleeps: espresso at the counter in the morning, pasta at midday, pizza at night. A bar that is also a restaurant and a pizzeria, the way it used to be.
The menu changes little, and that suits us: we would rather do ten things well than a hundred halfway. The pasta is bronze-cut, fish arrives fresh several times a week, vegetables follow the season.

Rome is a city of passers-by and of neighbourhoods at the same time. We like it when a local family sits at one table and someone who arrived that morning with a suitcase sits at the next. That is why the menu reads in nine languages: just scan the QR code.

posts.title: Real carbonara: four ingredients and no shortcuts
posts.excerpt: Guanciale, egg yolks, pecorino romano and pepper. No cream, no garlic, no onion. Here is how we make it, and why.
body: Carbonara is the dish Romans argue about most, and that makes sense: there are only four ingredients, so each one shows immediately. If one of them is mediocre, nothing can save the plate.
## Guanciale, not pancetta

Guanciale comes from the pig's cheek. It is sweeter and fattier than pancetta, and it behaves differently in the pan: the fat melts and becomes the real sauce. We cut it into strips half a centimetre thick and render it over medium heat, without rushing, until the lean part is crisp and the fat is translucent.
## The cream is made without cream

Egg yolks, pecorino romano grated to order and coarsely ground black pepper. Whisk them cold, then loosen with a ladle of pasta water. The pan must be off the heat when the pasta goes in: it is the residual warmth that binds the sauce, not the flame. Too hot and the egg sets into an omelette.
## Spaghetti or rigatoni
We serve it with spaghetti, because the sauce coats them evenly. Rigatoni work just as well and hold the sauce inside: it is a matter of taste, not of rules.
One last tip: grind the pepper fresh and toast it for a moment in the pan. That is the difference between a good plate and one you remember.

posts.title: Roman or Neapolitan pizza: what really changes
posts.excerpt: Tall crust or thin edge, hotter or cooler oven, different doughs. A short guide to choosing the one you prefer.
body: Anyone walking into a pizzeria in Rome meets two different schools, and neither is better than the other: they are two ideas of pizza.
## Roman: thin and crisp

Roman pizza has a very thin base, rolled out with a pin, and a low edge. It bakes at a slightly lower temperature for longer, so it comes out dry and crisp right to the middle. It is the one you can eat with your hands without it folding over.
## Neapolitan: a tall, soft crust

Neapolitan pizza is stretched by hand, leaving the air in the rim, which puffs up in the oven into a tall, open crust. It bakes very briefly at a very high temperature, stays soft, and should be eaten at once, with a fork if needed.
## What we serve

At Bar Capri we work a dough that matures for twenty-four hours at medium hydration: the result sits in between, with a crust that is present but not exaggerated, and a thin, well-baked centre. It is, we think, the pizza that eats best at the end of a long day.
For guests who cannot eat gluten we prepare a certified base, baked separately to avoid contamination.

posts.title: Eating gluten free in Rome: what to ask before you order
posts.excerpt: Three questions worth asking anywhere, and how gluten-free dishes are prepared here.
body: Anyone with coeliac disease knows the problem is not finding a place with gluten-free pasta, but understanding how they cook it. Here is what is worth asking everywhere, not only here.
## First question: where do they boil the pasta?
If gluten-free pasta boils in the same water as the regular one, the dish is not safe. It needs its own pot and clean water. Here, gluten-free pasta has its own pot and its own utensils.
## Second question: how do they bake the pizza?
A gluten-free base cannot go onto the same oven floor where a wheat dough has just been stretched. We bake ours in a dedicated tin and handle it with separate peels.
## Third question: who prepares it?
The work surface and a change of gloves matter too. No serious cook takes this question badly: if the kitchen is set up for it, the answer comes back straight away and precise.
## What is on the menu

Pizza, pasta, a dessert of the day and gluten-free beer, all with certified ingredients. We are not an entirely gluten-free kitchen, and we say so plainly: anyone with severe coeliac disease deserves honest information, not a vague reassurance.

posts.title: Eating well near Termini: how to avoid the traps
posts.excerpt: The station area has plenty of tourist traps and a few excellent tables. Four signs that tell them apart.
body: There are always places around a station that live on passing trade: you eat there once and never return. But the Esquilino is also a lived-in neighbourhood with a tradition of real trattorias. Here is how to spot them.
## The menu is short
A kitchen offering eighty dishes is not cooking all of them to order. A short menu, with a few daily specials, is nearly always a good sign.
## Prices are displayed and clear
Cover charge, service and any extras should be written down. If the price of fish is given only per hundred grams without the weight of a portion, ask what it will come to before you order.
## Nobody invites you in from the street
Staff stopping passers-by on the pavement is the most reliable sign that a place needs to fill up fast. Good tables have people sitting at them, not standing outside the door.
## There are local customers
This is the best test of all: if at lunchtime you see people who work nearby, the value for money holds up. Look at what is on their plates and order that.
We are at Via Principe Amedeo 78/80, five minutes on foot from the station. The menu is the one we always serve, and you can read the prices on this site before you even walk in.
